title: Re-evaluating Isolate.exit sacrifice for the flat ResultSet (rejected)
impact: Large read results (`>= 256 KB` estimated) use `Isolate.exit` **sacrifice** — a zero-copy heap transfer that kills the worker (a reader respawn) to avoid the `SendPort.send` graph copy. The founding measurement (exp 082) predates Dart 2.15 isolate groups, where `SendPort.send` now **shares** immutable leaves (strings/ints) across the hop and only copies the mutable structural graph — so send's cost tracks structural slot count, not bytes. This re-evaluated two changes: retire sacrifice (send-always), or re-trigger on structural slot count instead of estimated bytes. A transport check (`native_vs_heap_send.dart`, self-contained) confirms the model: a heap `Uint8List` send blows up with size (203-272 us at 512-731 KB) while a native-backed view sends cheaply (23-44 us) — send is only expensive to the extent the payload is mutable/copyable. The sacrifice A/B (via a reverted `RESQLITE_SACRIFICE_THRESHOLD` define) shows send faster-or-level across the practical numeric range and winning **large on text** (149 vs 438 us at 1000 rows — strings share on send, sacrifice respawns for a copy it never needed); sacrifice edges ahead only above **~32k structural slots**, by a noisy ~3-4%. **Both changes rejected:** send-always would regress the high-structural-count tail where sacrifice still wins; a slot-count trigger adds accounting complexity a ~3-4% noisy margin doesn't pay for (estimated bytes already correlates with slot count). The run also documents a confound — per-process repeated sacrifice respawns accumulate and bias the sacrifice lane, so this A/B can't cleanly isolate a single sacrifice-vs-send at a fixed size. Rejected; publication-only. Reopen with a clean single-shot per-process harness, or a production profile showing results clustering in the send-favored range.
